extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic theology; clergy and informed lay readers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Catholic doctrinal standards and theological distinctions concerning God’s salvific will, the distribution of grace, the fate of unbaptized infants and heathens, and the nature of predestination. Includes scriptural, patristic, and magisterial support and objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralitas sensuum in Scriptural interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Augustine’s doctrine that Scripture admits a plurality of literal senses (pluralitas sensuum) so that, over and above the sensus obvius, an exegete may read additional truths into a passage provided the several interpretations are not contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that multiple non-contradictory readings are within the inspiration of the Holy Ghost; reconciliation of apparent contradictions may rely on distinctions such as voluntas antecedens and consequens. Example: different readings of 1 Tim. II,4 can be reconciled by distinguishing antecedent vs consequent divine will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: voluntas antecedens vs voluntas consequens
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological distinction between God’s antecedent (antecedens) will (what He wills in general) and consequent (consequens) will (what He wills given particular circumstances), used to reconcile universal-sounding scriptural statements with particular outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to statements like 'God wills all men to be saved': antecedently God wills universal salvation; consequently (given secondary causes, justice, qualifications) some may be damned. Analogy: a judge antecedently wills all men to live, but consequently may will a murderer hanged when circumstances are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unbaptized infants and the universality of God’s salvific will
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis: the fate of unbaptized infants, though difficult, does not refute the universality of God’s saving will; the Church has not dogmatically defined their ultimate fate and theologians hold divergent opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys positions: Bellarmine’s claim that unbaptized infants are excluded (restricted and to be qualified); possibilities include baptism of blood, baptism of desire, God’s mercy cleansing original sin enabling a natural beatitude (Gutberlet), and the need for caution (no certain solution). Emphasizes responsibility of human agents (parents/priests) for administering Baptism and that exceptions (invincible ignorance, natural order) complicate culpability. Scriptural and magisterial affirmations of God’s universal mercy are cited as supporting that infants participate in divine mercy.

rubrics_metrics.name: God gives sufficient grace to all adult human beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Article assertion: in relation to adults, God manifests His saving will by bestowing sufficient grace upon all (sufficient graces are given to just, sinners, and heathen). God is not obliged to bestow efficacious grace to all, but sufficient grace (including gratia prima vocans) is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thesis I (de fide): God gives just men sufficient grace to keep His commandments; sufficiency is evidenced by scripture (e.g., 'the commandments are not heavy') and patristic teaching. Church teaches sufficient grace is at their disposal when called (urgente praecepto); proximate vs remote sufficient grace distinction is noted (gratia proxime sufficiens vs gratia remote sufficiens). The theological argument: the state of grace implies claim to necessary graces; divine promises and 'ad impossibile nemo tenetur' support the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ordinary and obdurate sinners re: sufficiency of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis II: (1) ordinary sinners always receive sufficient grace to avoid mortal sin and do penance; (2) God never entirely withdraws His grace even from obdurate sinners, though He may withhold greater graces in punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines ordinary sinner (lost sanctifying grace via grievous sin but not hardened) vs obdurate sinner (will hardened by repeated malice). Scriptural, patristic, and Thomistic supports: God provides initial/remote grace (gratia initialis sive parva) and grace proper to the law; the Fathers hold the light of grace is never wholly extinguished in this life. Rigorist position that God completely withdraws grace is rejected; final culpability lies with the sinner's own malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heathens receive sufficient graces for salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis III: those to whom the Gospel has not reached (the 'heathens') receive sufficient grace to know the truth and be saved; it is certain that God does not permit anyone to perish for want of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from 1 Tim. II,4 and other scriptural texts, Fathers, and magisterial condemnations of contrary Jansenist propositions. Discusses two explanatory theories: fides explicita (explicit faith: God somehow provides full explicit knowledge — via interior illumination, apostle, angel — seen as less plausible) and fides implicita (implicit faith/fides in voto: undeveloped desire to believe suffices for most dogmas). Also discusses role of natural reason and traditional instruction in providing explicit knowledge of God and retribution; cautions that the precise divine means remain ultimately with God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of types/objects of predestination
rubrics_metrics.description: Predestination can mean: predestination to receive certain graces (praedestinatio ad gratiam tantum), predestination to enjoy eternal happiness/glory without regard to merits (praedestinatio ad gloriam tantum), or predestination to both grace and glory (complete/adequate predestination). The dogma of predestination primarily concerns the adequate (complete) predestination to grace and glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historical and theological usage: Trent calls predestination a 'hidden mystery'; Augustine’s formulation: predestination as foreknowledge and preparation of gifts by which the saved are most certainly delivered. The text distinguishes incomplete/inadequate predestination (separate treatment of grace and glory) from the full doctrine, and indicates debate among theologians about praedestinatio ad gloriam tantum. Emphasizes that predestination pertains to God’s inscrutable decrees and the unequal distribution of efficacious grace is the theological locus of the mystery.
